The scent of spiced wine and roasted pheasant hung heavy in the air, a cloying perfume of death to one for whom the gallows-tree was already being prepared, and Elara found herself wishing the entire farcical affair were done. The waiting was a torment worse than any executioner’s rope; a slow, grinding torture of the nerves that made the final snap seem a welcome relief. The feast had been a shimmering, beautiful horror, full of laughter as sharp as broken glass, and now the guests were settled, their faces flushed with wine and anticipation, ready for the evening’s true entertainment. Her judge, the Magistrate Lord Valerius, was a man sculpted from pale marble and ennui, who lounged in a high-backed chair, fingering a jeweled letter opener as if it were a scepter. Beside him stood the Warden, a mountain of scarred flesh and silent menace whose only purpose seemed to be to loom.

The court, if such it could be called, convened with no ceremony save for Lord Valerius waving a languid hand. He was a man of exquisite tastes, of delicate sensibilities, and of the most profound and unbending cruelty. The proceedings began with him directing a bored, yet piercing, gaze upon the prisoner.

“The matter is simple, is it not?” he said, his voice a silken drawl. “A bauble was purloined from my private collection; a rather fetching sapphire known as the Widow’s Tear. And here you stand.”

“A pretty thing indeed, my lord,” Elara replied, her voice clear and steady despite the tremor in her hands. “Though I confess it looked far better against my own skin than it ever did gathering dust in your coffer.”

A ripple of scandalized amusement went through the assembled nobles, but Lord Valerius only raised a single, perfectly sculpted eyebrow. “Insolence from the condemned is so rarely original. A pity. Your name, girl?”

“I am called Elara. Is your lordship displeased with it?”

“On the contrary; it has a certain rustic charm. Tell me, Elara, were you acting alone when you desecrated my sanctum, or were you the agent of some jealous rival?”

“I am an agent only of my own empty stomach, my lord,” she said with a slight, mocking curtsy. “Your rivals, I should imagine, have better sense than to hire a common thief.”

“She admits it!” cried a portly baron from the side, eager to prove his attentiveness. “She admits to being a common thief!”

“I admit to being common, certainly,” Elara shot back, her eyes flashing. “It is a condition far preferable to being a common fool.”

The baron turned a shade of plum, and Lord Valerius sighed, a sound of profound theatrical weariness. “This is becoming tiresome. You stole the jewel, that much is clear. You display no remorse, which is an affront to good taste. Have you any reason why the usual sentence should not be carried out immediately?”

“None that your lordship would comprehend,” she answered.

“Excellent. I do so detest long, drawn-out justifications.” He set the letter opener down with a soft click and picked up a scroll of parchment, upon which he made a small, elegant mark with a silver quill. “The sentence is, as always in such trivial matters, quite straightforward: a short drop and a sudden stop. Warden, you may proceed.”

The great brute of a man took a step forward, his shadow falling over Elara like a shroud. Her heart hammered against her ribs, a wild bird trapped in a cage of bone; but her face remained a mask of defiance. Just as the Warden reached for her arm, a new voice cut through the room, as cold and sharp as a shard of ice.

“Valerius, must you? The musicians are arriving for the midnight recital, and I will not have their harmonies disturbed by the uncouth sounds of a public strangling.”

All eyes turned to the doorway, where Lady Seraphina stood, a vision of frost and silk. She was the Magistrate’s wife, her face a mask of bored indifference, and she surveyed the scene not as a matter of life and death, but as an irritating disruption to her evening’s schedule. The Warden froze, his hand hovering in mid-air.

Lord Valerius’s placid expression tightened almost imperceptibly. “My dear, we are concluding a matter of justice.”

“You are concluding a piece of theater, husband, and the timing is inconvenient. We have guests from the Southern Isles; what will they think if the first thing they hear is the gurgling of a dying peasant? It is utterly provincial.”

“The law must be served,” Valerius said, though his voice lacked its earlier conviction.

“Then let it be served tomorrow, when there is nothing better to do. I will not have my recital spoiled by your grim little hobbies. Have the girl taken to the oubliette, and see that she is quiet. Her very existence is a blemish on the evening.”

She did not wait for a reply, but swept from the room with a rustle of satin, leaving a stunned silence in her wake. Lord Valerius stared after her, his jaw set, a flicker of genuine anger in his cold eyes. He took a slow, deliberate breath, then turned his gaze back to the prisoner.

“It seems you have earned a reprieve,” he said, his voice dripping with venom. “Do not mistake it for mercy. Warden, do as her ladyship commands. Lock her away. We shall finish this at a more convenient hour.”

The Warden nodded once, his face impassive, and his heavy hand finally closed upon Elara’s arm. As he led her away, she glanced back at the Magistrate, who had already picked up his jeweled letter opener and was examining its facets with renewed, if slightly ruffled, interest, as if she were already forgotten.

His highness stopped, his hands clenched into white-knuckled fists, and his face, already a study in malevolence, contorted into a mask of such pure, distilled hatred that it was a wonder the very air did not curdle around him. He said nothing more, however; he had lost this round, and he knew it, but his terrible grin returned, wider and more menacing than before, promising a future reckoning that would be all the more dreadful for its delay.

Sir Norman, for his part, allowed himself to be led away without resistance; for what was the use of it? He cast one last, lingering look at the queen, who had already resumed her posture of graceful indifference, as if the entire affair had been a momentary, and rather vulgar, interruption to her thoughts. Had she saved him out of some hidden well of pity, or was it merely the caprice of a woman who would not be gainsaid, even in the matter of a man’s last moments? The question puzzled him, and the not-unpleasant sting of it was a strange companion to the cold certainty of his doom. He was a dead man, merely taking a rather more scenic route to the grave than he had previously anticipated.

The guards led him not down into the bowels of the earth, as he had expected, but along a succession of corridors so splendidly appointed that he felt he must be on his way to a royal levée rather than a prison cell. They passed through galleries hung with priceless tapestries depicting hunts and battles of a bygone age, and antechambers where gilded clocks ticked away the moments with serene, unhurried grace. The air was thick with the scent of beeswax and wilted flowers, the ghosts of a thousand courtly evenings. It was a palace of contradictions, of breathtaking beauty and mortal peril, a place where one might be murdered with a jeweled dagger or a well-aimed epigram.

At last, they stopped before a heavy, oak door, studded with iron nails in a spiraling pattern. One of the guards produced a key, as long and ornate as a ceremonial scepter, and turned it in the lock with a groan of metal that echoed in the silent hall. The door swung inward, revealing not the squalor of a dungeon, but a small, circular chamber, surprisingly clean and utterly bare. High above, a single, narrow slit of a window, heavily barred, showed a sliver of the star-strewn, inky sky. There was no furniture save for a stone bench that was part of the wall itself, and a thick iron ring set into the floor at its center.

“You will wait here,” said the first guard, his voice a low, gravelly rumble that seemed to come from the depths of his chest.

“A change of scenery, if not of fortune,” Sir Norman remarked, stepping inside. “I am bound to thank her majesty for the accommodation. It is a decided improvement on the Black Chamber, I imagine.”

The guard did not smile, but a flicker of something that might have been grim amusement passed through his eyes. “Her majesty’s whims are not for us to question,” he said. “Nor are they for you to understand. Be glad of the stone walls, sir. They will muffle the sounds from the trial chamber.”

With that, the heavy door was pulled shut, the key turned once more with a deafening finality, and Sir Norman was left alone in the sudden, profound silence. He stood for a moment in the center of the room, listening to the guards’ footsteps recede until they were swallowed by the vastness of the palace. Then he went to the stone bench and sat down, the cold of it seeping through his clothes. He was a prisoner, doubly so; trapped not only within these stone walls but within the web of this mad court’s incomprehensible justice. He rested his head back against the wall, the rough-hewn stone a coarse comfort, and closed his eyes.

He tried to piece together the whirlwind of the last few hours; the flight from the city, the encounter with the highwayman, the farcical dinner, and the still more farcical trial. It was all a fever dream from which he would surely wake; and yet, the chill of the stone beneath him was undeniably real. He thought of the queen, that impossible creature of ice and fire. She had signed his death warrant with a hand as steady as a surgeon’s, her face a mask of sublime boredom. Then, with a few imperious words, she had granted him this brief, inexplicable stay of execution. Was it cruelty? Was it a game? Or was it something else, something he could not dare to name, a flicker of humanity buried so deep beneath the layers of queenship that it could only emerge in such oblique and contradictory ways? He found, to his own surprise, that he hoped it was the latter; for a man about to die, it was a strange and useless thing to hope for, and yet he could not help himself.

Time passed, measured only by the slow, almost imperceptible crawl of the stars across the sliver of sky visible through his window. He must have dozed, for he was startled awake by a faint, distant sound; a woman’s voice, raised not in a scream, but in a high, theatrical wail of protest. The second trial, he realized, must have begun. Lady Castlemaine was now facing her judges. He strained his ears, but the stone walls did their work as the guard had promised, and all that reached him were the faintest murmurs and echoes, the ghost of a drama unfolding elsewhere. He pictured the scene; the dwarf grinning on his high-backed chair, the duke preening with prosecutorial zeal, the courtiers fluttering like nervous moths around a deadly flame. And the queen, sitting still and silent, a beautiful, deadly idol at the heart of the storm. He wondered what secrets the poisoning of a duchess might hold, and found he did not much care. It was all part of the same grand, grotesque pageant.

Back in the great hall, the scene was much as Sir Norman had imagined it. A woman had been brought before the green table, a woman of perhaps thirty years, whose beauty was of that frantic, desperate sort which is already beginning to look over its shoulder at the ghost of what it once was. Her hair, a magnificent cascade of auburn, was in disarray, and her fine silk gown was torn at the shoulder, but she held her head high, her eyes flashing with a mixture of terror and defiance. This was Lady Castlemaine.

“My lady,” the duke began, his voice dripping with a bogus sympathy that was more insulting than open contempt, “you stand accused of a most heinous crime. The murder, by poison, of the beloved Duchess of Sutherland. A grievous charge, a charge that pains me to the very soul to articulate.”

“Then do not articulate it, your grace!” she retorted, her voice trembling but sharp. “For it is a lie, a foul and venomous lie, and you know it!”

His highness, Prince Caliban, leaned forward, his elbows on the table and his chin in his hands, his grin stretching so wide it seemed to threaten the integrity of his face. “Oh, we do not know it at all, my dear lady,” he chortled. “In fact, we have evidence to the contrary. Have we not, my Lord Duke?”

“Indeed, we have, your highness,” the duke said, producing a small, folded piece of paper with a flourish. “A letter, in your own hand, addressed to an apothecary in the city, detailing the purchase of a certain quantity of wolfsbane, to be administered, and I quote, ‘for a troublesome greyhound that has fallen from favor.’ A rather poetic description of the duchess, would you not agree?”

A gasp went around the room. Lady Castlemaine’s face went white as bleached bone. “That letter… it is a forgery! I never wrote such a thing!”

“And yet,” the dwarf said softly, his eyes glittering like chips of obsidian, “the apothecary confirms the sale. And the duchess’s own physician confirms the cause of death. Wolfsbane. A most unpleasant end, I am told. Cramps, convulsions, a paralytic rigor while the heart is still beating. Did she suffer greatly, my lady? One imagines you would have stayed to watch.”

“You are a monster!” she shrieked, all pretense of composure gone. “A vile, twisted little goblin!”

“And you are a poisoner,” Caliban replied with a shrug. “We all have our little failings. The question now is not whether you did it, for that is as plain as the nose on my… well, as plain as day. The question is, why? The duchess was your friend, was she not?”

“She was no friend of mine!” Lady Castlemaine cried, goaded beyond reason. “She was a snake, a prattling, self-satisfied cow who took what was not hers!”

“Ah!” said the duke, seizing upon the admission. “And what did she take, my lady? A lover, perhaps? Or something more… tangible?”

Lady Castlemaine’s eyes darted wildly around the room, from the duke’s smug face to the dwarf’s eager one, and finally to the silent, immobile figure of the queen. For the first time that night, the queen’s posture had changed. She was no longer listless; she was still, but it was the stillness of a hunting panther, every fiber of her being attuned to the words being spoken.

“It was the Sutherland necklace,” Lady Castlemaine whispered, her voice barely audible. “Her majesty promised it to me. The duchess charmed it from her, whispered lies in her ear about me…”

“The necklace?” the duke repeated, his brow furrowed in mock confusion. “You murdered a woman for a piece of jewelry?”

“It was my right! It was to be mine!” she sobbed, her fury collapsing into a heap of self-pity. “And she was not the only one who wronged me! You all did! You sit here in judgment, but you are all as guilty as I!” Her wild eyes fell upon the duke. “You, your grace! You speak of poison, but what of the poison you pour into the prince’s ear every day? What of the plots you hatch together? What of the night you came to me, seeking my help to procure a sleeping draught, a strong one, you said, for her majesty herself!”

A profound, shocked silence fell upon the room. Even the courtiers, hardened to every kind of scandal, seemed to hold their breath. The duke’s face, which had been a mask of judicial severity, turned a mottled, unhealthy shade of purple.

“This is… this is madness!” he stammered, his dignity deserting him entirely. “The woman is raving! She seeks to drag us all down with her!”

But the dwarf was not looking at the duke. He was looking at Lady Castlemaine, and the grin on his face was gone, replaced by an expression of cold, calculating interest.

“Did he now?” Prince Caliban said, his voice dangerously quiet. “A sleeping draught, you say? For the queen? Do go on, my lady. This is becoming a most interesting trial indeed. Perhaps your memory, so faulty a moment ago, has improved.”

“He said,” Lady Castlemaine went on, sensing she had found a new, and perhaps more powerful, weapon than innocence, “he said the queen’s humors were… unpredictable. That her sleeplessness made her erratic. He said a long rest would be a kindness, to her and to the kingdom. He said you, your highness, would be grateful for such a service.”

The duke looked as if he might faint. He opened his mouth to speak, but only a dry, croaking sound came out. All eyes were now on him, a hundred pairs of eyes, curious, accusatory, and hungry for his downfall.

The queen had not moved. Her long lashes still shadowed her eyes, her face was still a pale, perfect oval in the candlelight. But one of her hands, which had been lying limply in her lap, had slowly, almost unconsciously, clenched into a fist, the knuckles showing white against the deep purple of her velvet gown.

His highness, Prince Caliban, let the silence stretch for a full minute, savoring the duke’s palpable terror like a connoisseur tasting a rare vintage. He glanced from the trembling duke to the desperate Lady Castlemaine, and then, for a brief, unreadable moment, his eyes met the queen’s across the room. What passed between them in that instant, no one could say, but when the dwarf turned back to the proceedings, his grin had returned, more terrible than ever.

“Well, well, well,” he said, rubbing his hands together. “Treason and poison, all in one evening. We are truly blessed. It seems our docket has become a little more crowded. My Lord Duke, you have shown such an aptitude for prosecution, it would be a shame not to let you experience the process from the other side. Guards! Place the duke under arrest. He shall have the honor of being tried immediately after our dear Lady Castlemaine has received her sentence.”

The duke let out a strangled gasp. “Your highness! This is an outrage! A travesty! I am your most loyal servant!”

“And you will serve me still,” the dwarf cackled, “as an object lesson in the swiftness of our justice. As for you, my lady,” he said, turning his attention back to the now weeping woman, “for the crime of murdering the Duchess of Sutherland, a crime to which you have all but confessed, the sentence is the same as it was for our spy friend. A trip to the Black Chamber, and a sharp, decisive meeting with the headsman. But! In light of your… most helpful testimony regarding the duke, we are inclined to be merciful. Your execution shall be swift. His, I think, will be somewhat more prolonged. We have certain instruments in the lower levels that have not been used in some time, and it would be a pity to let them rust.”

He paused, his eyes sweeping the room, daring anyone to challenge him. The queen remained silent, a statue of disdain. The duke, now held between two unsmiling guards, seemed to have shrunk, his face a ruin of its former pompous glory. Lady Castlemaine had collapsed to her knees, sobbing without restraint.

“So it is decreed,” the prince concluded, his voice rising to a triumphant shout. “Let the sentences be carried out! Together! The spy, the poisoner, and the traitor! Bring them all to the Black Chamber at once! We shall make a night of it! A festival of justice!” He clapped his hands together with a sound like two dry bones smacking, and broke into a peal of laughter so wild and unhinged that it sent a shiver down the spine of everyone present. The queen alone seemed unaffected, but as the guards moved to obey, she slowly, deliberately, lifted her long lashes, and her dark, brilliant eyes, filled with a light that was neither cold nor bored but something far more dangerous, fixed themselves upon the door through which Sir Norman Kingsley had been led away.
